videos.title: LUCID DREAMING vs SLEEP PARALYSIS
videos.description:
It's 3 AM. Your eyes open, but you can't move. There's a weight on your chest and a dark figure standing in the corner of the room.

That's sleep paralysis. And it happens in almost exactly the same place in your brain as the opposite experience: lucid dreaming, where you know you're dreaming and can fly, walk through walls, and talk to the people in your dream.

In this video we put them head to head: what REM sleep actually does to your body, how scientists proved people can be aware inside a dream using nothing but eye movements, the 2021 experiment where researchers asked sleeping people maths questions and got answers back, why the "shadow figure" shows up in cultures all over the world, and which one you're statistically more likely to experience.

CHAPTERS
0:00 3 AM: you can't move
1:01 Part 1: Where they both come from (REM sleep)
2:13 Part 2: Lucid dreaming
4:04 Part 3: Sleep paralysis
5:52 Part 4: The day scientists talked to dreamers
6:55 Part 5: The twist
7:56 The verdict
8:41 Which one would you keep?

Have you had a lucid dream? Sleep paralysis? Or both? Tell me in the comments.

If sleep paralysis happens often, or comes with extreme daytime sleepiness, talk to a doctor. It can be linked to sleep disorders like narcolepsy. This video is for education, not medical advice.

SOURCES
- Saunders et al. (2016), "Lucid dreaming incidence: A quality effects meta-analysis of 50 years of research", Consciousness and Cognition
- Konkoly et al. (2021), "Real-time dialogue between experimenters and dreamers during REM sleep", Current Biology

Witaj, Przyjacielu, Przyjaciółko… 🌿

Zapraszam Cię dzisiaj w niezwykłą podróż. Nie będzie to podróż w odległe miejsca, ale podróż w głąb samego siebie.

Carl Gustav Jung, szwajcarski psychiatra i twórca psychologii analitycznej, zwracał uwagę na to, że każdy człowiek ma w sobie również cień.

Czym jest nasz cień?

To te części naszej osobowości, których nie zawsze chcemy dostrzegać. Mogą to być emocje, pragnienia, lęki, zranienia, poczucie krzywdy, wstyd, zazdrość, złość, ale również nasze niewykorzystane możliwości, siła i talenty, których nie pozwoliliśmy sobie rozwinąć.

Często przez całe życie uczymy się pokazywać światu tylko tę część siebie, którą inni akceptują. Ukrywamy łzy, tłumimy emocje, udajemy, że coś nas nie boli. Czasami nawet sami przed sobą nie przyznajemy się do tego, co naprawdę czujemy.

Ale to, czego nie chcemy zobaczyć, nie zawsze przestaje w nas istnieć.

Praca z cieniem nie polega na ocenianiu siebie ani na szukaniu w sobie czegoś złego. Polega na odwadze poznania siebie w pełniejszy sposób.

Nie musisz dzisiaj niczego naprawiać. Nie musisz nikomu niczego udowadniać. Wystarczy, że pozwolisz sobie zadać kilka szczerych pytań.

Co we mnie domaga się zauważenia? Jakie emocje próbuję ukryć? Czego w sobie nie akceptuję? Jakie doświadczenia wciąż wpływają na moje reakcje?

Pamiętaj, że cień nie jest Twoim wrogiem. Jest zaproszeniem do poznania tych obszarów siebie, które być może przez długi czas pozostawały niezauważone.

Dzisiaj spróbujemy spojrzeć na siebie z życzliwością, bez osądzania i bez poczucia winy.

Bo prawdziwe poznanie siebie zaczyna się wtedy, kiedy przestajemy uciekać przed własną prawdą.

On October 28, 2026, the Bank of Canada raised its policy rate to 2.5% - its first increase since July 2023 - while growth was only modest. On November 5, 2026, Governor Tiff Macklem told a Senate committee that inflation had been around 3% since April 2026 and was expected to rise to about 3.5% by the end of 2026, with oil prices higher for longer. Prices rising fast, output not booming: was that the spending side or the production side? In about 16 minutes you'll build the one picture that answers that question - aggregate demand and aggregate supply - and learn the fingerprint test that diagnoses any headline.

WHAT YOU'LL LEARN
- The two axes of the big model: the price level up the side, real output across the bottom - and how one crossing sets both at once
- Aggregate demand: total planned spending by households, firms, governments, and foreigners - and why it slopes down (the wealth effect, the interest rate effect, and the net export effect, each told as a story)

videos.title: The Business Cycle Explained: Four Phases, Rising Slowly and Falling Fast
videos.description:
The business cycle is the repeated sequence of expansions and contractions in the economy as a whole. For a few years, output, jobs and incomes rise together. Then, for some months, they fall together. All of this happens on top of long run growth: a dashed long run path, and a solid line for what actually happens, rising above the path, dropping below it and crossing it again. Three things follow. The cycle is economy wide, so most industries rise and fall at the same time. It repeats, but not on a timetable. And it is marked by its turning points, the peaks and the troughs, rather than by any single growth rate.

The cycle has four phases. In the expansion, output and jobs grow, firms add shifts and credit is easy to get. The peak is the turning point where activity stops rising, and it tends to arrive when conditions feel best, which is why so few people see it coming. In the contraction, activity falls, firms cut hours and then jobs, and spending drops; when the fall is deep, broad and lasting, it is a recession. The trough is the lowest point, where unemployment is often still rising. The recovery is the early part of the next expansion, and it lasts until output is back at its old peak.

The real cycle is not a smooth wave. Since 1949 America has had eleven complete expansions, as dated by the National Bureau of Economic Research. The shortest lasted twelve months, from July 1980 to July 1981. The longest lasted 128, from June 2009 to February 2020. On average an expansion lasted about 67 months, more than five years, and a contraction about ten. Out of the 944 months from January 1948 to August 2026, about thirteen percent were months of recession, a little more than one month in eight. An economy rises slowly for years and falls fast for months. The current expansion began after the trough in April 2020, and by August 2026 it had run 76 months with no peak announced.

The parts of the economy move together. Across the twelve recessions since 1948, real GDP fell on average about two and three quarter percent from its high to its low. Household spending fell less, under two percent. Industrial production fell almost nine percent, and investment by businesses and home builders about seventeen. On average investment fell more than six times as much as output, and it fell further than output in every one of the twelve. In ten of them household spending fell less than output.
